PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 74 — Lesson 98: Heart Failure Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize heart failure as a clinical syndrome, establish the patient’s baseline phenotype and trajectory, distinguish congestion from hypoperfusion, identify decompensation triggers, support guideline-directed treatment and monitoring, and recognize when dyspnea or edema requires emergency rather than outpatient care.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate heart-failure syndrome from an isolated low ejection fraction, edema, or medication list.
  • Use the concepts of HFrEF, HFpEF, congestion, and perfusion to organize assessment without oversimplifying the diagnosis.
  • Perform a focused differential for dyspnea, edema, fatigue, and weight change and identify common decompensation triggers.
  • Explain the roles of disease-modifying therapy, diuretics, kidney and potassium monitoring, self-management support, and transitions of care.
  • Recognize pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, ischemia, dangerous arrhythmia, severe hypotension, and other emergency patterns.

Part 1 — Heart Failure Is a Syndrome, Not an EF Label

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs caused by structural or functional cardiac abnormality, often involving elevated filling pressures, impaired forward flow, or both. Dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, abdominal fullness, reduced exercise tolerance, crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, and rapid weight change can support the diagnosis but are not specific by themselves.

HFrEF generally involves reduced systolic ejection; causes include ischemic injury, cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, toxins, and persistent tachyarrhythmia. HFpEF involves impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures despite preserved ejection fraction; hypertension, aging, obesity, diabetes, CKD, atrial fibrillation, and valvular disease often contribute. Both can cause serious congestion, hospitalization, and disability. A preserved EF does not mean the patient has no heart failure.

Part 2 — First Question at Every Visit: What Has Changed?

Compare today with the patient’s known baseline. Ask about exertional tolerance, dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, nocturnal symptoms, weight trend, edema, abdominal fullness, appetite, dizziness, syncope, chest discomfort, palpitations, urine output, BP and heart-rate readings, medication changes, missed doses, sodium exposure, NSAID use, alcohol or stimulant exposure, infection, recent hospitalization, and support at home. The pattern and rate of change are often more informative than one isolated sign.

Examine vital signs, oxygenation when appropriate, work of breathing, mental status, temperature, perfusion, lung findings, JVP when interpretable, edema, abdomen, weight, peripheral warmth, rhythm, and signs of infection or thrombosis. Review kidney function, electrolytes, natriuretic peptides, ECG, imaging, or other testing when the clinical question warrants it. A biomarker or echocardiogram supports care; neither replaces history and examination.

Part 3 — Congestion Versus Hypoperfusion

Congestion reflects elevated filling pressures and may appear as pulmonary symptoms, orthopnea, rales, elevated JVP, edema, ascites, abdominal discomfort, or rapid weight gain. Hypoperfusion reflects inadequate forward flow and may appear as cool extremities, altered mentation, oliguria, severe fatigue, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension, or worsening end-organ function. A patient can be congested, hypoperfused, both, or neither.

Wet-and-cold physiology—congestion plus hypoperfusion—is particularly concerning. A patient who is breathless and edematous but also hypotensive, confused, cool, or oliguric may be deteriorating rapidly. This is not a routine outpatient diuretic-refill situation. The FNP’s judgment about safe setting is more important than assigning a perfect phenotype label.

Part 4 — Preserve the Differential for Dyspnea and Edema

Heart failure may coexist with COPD, asthma, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia, CKD, liver disease, venous disease, obesity/deconditioning, anemia, thyroid disease, medication effect, or malignancy. Bilateral edema alone does not prove HF; unilateral swelling needs a different differential. Crackles alone do not prove cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Ask which physiology best explains the whole story.

New chest pressure, pleuritic pain, fever, hemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling, sudden dyspnea, wheeze, tachyarrhythmia, severe anemia symptoms, or focal neurologic symptoms change the workup and disposition. Do not anchor on a known diagnosis when the presentation is new or different.

Part 5 — Identify the Trigger, Not Only the Fluid

Common causes of decompensation include missed or inaccessible medication, high sodium intake, NSAIDs and other medication effects, kidney dysfunction, atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, uncontrolled hypertension, infection, anemia, thyroid disease, alcohol or stimulant exposure, pulmonary disease, progressive valvular disease, and inadequate follow-up after discharge. Treating congestion without identifying a precipitant invites repeat decompensation.

Ask the patient to show medication bottles and describe a usual day. Pharmacy gaps, confusing discharge instructions, inability to afford a diuretic, food insecurity, limited bathroom access, cognitive difficulty, language barriers, and lack of a scale can all determine whether the plan works. Social context is hemodynamic safety context.

Part 6 — Medication Principles and Monitoring

Diuretics primarily relieve volume congestion and symptoms. They do not substitute for disease-modifying treatment when such treatment is indicated. For many patients with chronic HFrEF, guideline-directed medical therapy includes therapies that target neurohormonal pathways and reduce adverse outcomes; contemporary strategies commonly include a renin-angiotensin system approach, an evidence-based beta blocker, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist when clinically appropriate. Selection, sequencing, and titration require review of BP, volume, eGFR, potassium, heart rate, contraindications, pregnancy potential, comorbidity, cost, access, and collaboration requirements.

A laboratory change after therapy adjustment is a signal to interpret, not an automatic reason to stop all therapy or ignore risk. Review timing, volume status, symptoms, BP, renal function, potassium, medication interactions, and indication. The FNP should use current guidelines and specialist support to maintain life-prolonging therapy when safe and to pause or escalate when hypotension, AKI, severe electrolyte disturbance, or decompensation makes outpatient adjustment unsafe.

Part 7 — Patient Education That Prevents Readmission

Teach each patient their baseline symptoms, weight-monitoring plan when appropriate, medication purpose, refill pathway, dietary and fluid instructions individualized to the care plan, activity limits, and exact signs that require a call, same-day visit, or emergency response. Use teach-back. A patient who understands the name of a diuretic but cannot identify worsening orthopnea, edema, or low-BP symptoms has not received adequate safety education.

Transition-of-care visits should occur promptly after hospitalization. Reconcile every medicine, clarify what changed and why, review laboratory orders, ensure access to a scale and medications, schedule cardiology or HF follow-up, assess home support, and document responsibility for pending tests. One of the strongest FNP interventions is making discharge instructions usable at home.

Part 8 — Referral, Advanced Care, and Goals

Expedited cardiology or heart-failure-team involvement is appropriate for new or uncertain HF, repeated decompensation, recurrent hospitalizations, difficult volume or medication management, advanced CKD, significant valvular disease, suspected cardiomyopathy, persistent symptoms despite treatment, device or advanced-therapy consideration, or high-risk arrhythmia. Referral does not replace primary care; the FNP coordinates diabetes, CKD, tobacco, vaccination, depression, frailty, and social needs.

Discuss prognosis, advance-care planning, and symptom priorities in a compassionate, developmentally appropriate way, particularly with advanced disease or repeated hospitalization. Goals-of-care conversations are not abandonment. They help align treatment intensity, symptom management, caregiver support, and emergency preferences with what matters to the patient.

Part 9 — Clinical Case: Congested and Hypoperfused

A 71-year-old with prior MI and EF 30% reports three days of orthopnea, rapid weight gain, edema, reduced urine output, and lightheadedness. Today the patient is tachypneic, hypotensive, and has crackles. FNP reasoning: the patient appears congested but may also be hypoperfused. Evaluate immediate stability and triggers such as ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, medication change, or AKI; emergency evaluation is safer than routine outpatient adjustment.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: Preserved EF Does Not Mean No HF

A 76-year-old with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea, edema, and an EF of 60%. FNP reasoning: preserved EF does not exclude heart failure. Consider HFpEF physiology, rate/rhythm, BP, renal function, valvular disease, pulmonary disease, medication effects, and volume status; organize diagnostic and cardiology follow-up rather than dismissing symptoms because EF is normal.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Trigger Hunt After Discharge

A 62-year-old returns two weeks after HF hospitalization with worsening edema. Medication review reveals a discontinued diuretic was never obtained, the patient is taking ibuprofen for dental pain, and no laboratory follow-up was completed. FNP reasoning: correct the transition failure, assess stability and kidney/potassium risk, clarify the medication plan, address pain safely, arrange timely monitoring, and close the loop with cardiology. Recurrent decompensation may be preventable when the actual barrier is found.

FNP High-Yield Framework: HEART

  1. H — Hear the trajectory: baseline, rapid change, dyspnea, weight, symptoms, medication access, and triggers.
  2. E — Evaluate congestion and perfusion: lungs, edema, JVP, BP, warmth, mentation, urine output, and oxygenation.
  3. A — Ask what else: ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, PE, renal/liver disease, anemia, pulmonary disease, and medication effects.
  4. R — Reconcile treatment: disease-modifying therapy, diuretics, labs, adverse effects, affordability, and self-management capacity.
  5. T — Transition and triage: emergency signs, post-discharge follow-up, referral, result ownership, and goals of care.

Take-Home Summary

Heart failure management is careful physiology plus reliable follow-up. At each visit, compare baseline and trajectory, identify congestion and hypoperfusion, investigate triggers, protect kidney and potassium safety, and ensure the patient can actually obtain and understand the plan. Severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, chest pain, syncope, hypotension, confusion, cool extremities, or oliguria signals urgent or emergency care.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace current heart-failure guidelines, medication labeling, titration protocols, cardiology consultation, advanced-care planning, or individualized emergency disposition. Suspected pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, acute coronary syndrome, dangerous arrhythmia, or unstable perfusion requires emergency evaluation.
